problems.statement: ED nurse understaffing is the cause of the ED length-of-stay rise (the client's explanation).

Inpatient discharges on the hospitalist medical wards moved later after the March 2026 rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first). Bed availability in the afternoon fell, and admitted patients board in the ED.
The rise in the headline measure is almost entirely ED boarding of admitted patients (about 3.0 of 3.2 h). ED work-up time, volume, acuity, admission rate and total inpatient capacity barely changed.

ED nurse workload strain, morale decline and leave-intent are real, but they are mostly a consequence of boarding. Boarders occupy 9-12 of 36 rooms and nurses give inpatient care, so the strain is not an independent staffing shortfall.

The discontinued provider-in-triage shift (1 May 2026) contributes to worse door-to-provider time and left-without-being-seen rates. It is a secondary front-end problem and does not explain the admitted-patient boarding rise.
Reduced evening bed-cleaning staff (from 1 Sept) may be adding to bed turnaround delay. Boarding had already risen by April, so it cannot be the origin, and there is no turnaround data after June.
Overall inpatient capacity or census pressure, or higher ED demand or acuity, drove the rise.
Post-decision delays in the discharge process (order to departure, transport) explain the later discharges.

causalClaims.from: Hospitalist rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first), March 2026
causalClaims.to: Later medical-ward discharge orders and departures
Afternoon bed shortage and ED boarding
Headline ED length of stay for admitted patients
ED nurse workload strain and morale decline, with no rooms for lobby patients
Earlier discharges and shorter boarding on 4 West
Worse door-to-provider time and higher left-without-being-seen rate

causalClaims.from: ED volume, acuity or inpatient occupancy change

actions.action: Scale the discharge-first rounding or huddle protocol to all four medical wards. Train all hospitalists and make it routine, for example by seeing likely discharges first or writing discharge orders before 09:30 or by noon.
actions.rationale: Within the pilot, huddle days on 4 West halved boarding (2.3 h vs 4.6 h). The comparison was effectively randomized by a pre-set rotation, and the mechanism fits the system-wide timeline.

actions.action: Have the CNO, hospitalist leadership and the COO jointly own a hospital-wide target for discharge timing and ED boarding, and report the boarding metric on the board scorecard. Keep the teaching meeting but resequence rounds.
actions.rationale: The origin is a cross-department scheduling choice that the ED cannot fix, and the hospitalist director's retention concern needs a design that avoids a return to the 07:00 start.

actions.action: Do not pause the 4 West huddle or float its charge nurse to the ED.
actions.rationale: The huddle is the one intervention with demonstrated effect on boarding, and pausing it would worsen the ED problem the float is meant to relieve.

actions.action: Do not fund travel nurses by deferring the two medical-ward case manager hires or reassigning the 4 West case manager.
actions.rationale: Case managers prepare the discharge lists the huddle depends on, and coverage is already below target.

actions.action: Approve the $1.46M eight-travel-nurse contract as the primary fix for ED length of stay.
actions.rationale: Staffing is at grid and vacancy is falling. Extra nurses would be absorbed by boarders and would not reduce the 3 h boarding increase.

actions.action: Reinstate the provider-in-triage shift, or an equivalent, to address door-to-provider time and left-without-being-seen rates.
actions.rationale: It addresses a real secondary front-end problem, but it is not the driver of admitted-patient length of stay, and hourly front-end data are lacking.

actions.action: Restore evening bed-turnaround reporting and check whether the reduction in bed-cleaning staff is adding delay.
actions.rationale: The effect is plausible but unmeasured, and the data are cheap to recover.

actions.action: Reverse the March rounding change entirely and return to the 07:00 start.
actions.rationale: The sequencing change is probably what matters, and a full reversal would risk losing hospitalists. Test a resequenced 09:30 start first.

nextEvidence: Hourly and monthly ED front-end series (door-to-provider, left-without-being-seen) against the 1 May triage-provider cut and boarding census, to size the secondary front-end effect
Restored evening bed-turnaround times (discharge departure to bed ready) since June, to test the evening bed-cleaning staff reduction
Results of extending the discharge-first protocol to more wards or all hospitalists, covering boarding hours, departures before 12:00, and hospitalist retention and satisfaction
output.summary: The rise in ED length of stay for admitted patients is a boarding problem, not an ED nursing shortage. About 3.0 of the 3.2 h increase is boarding. ED work-up time, volume, acuity, nurse hours per visit, vacancy and grid compliance are all flat or improved. Boarding began in March, when hospitalist rounding moved to 09:30 with new admissions first. Medical-ward discharges slid to the afternoon, and surgical wards did not change. A near-randomized 4 West pilot halved boarding. ED nurse strain is mostly downstream of boarders occupying rooms. Triage-provider loss is a secondary front-end issue. Recommend scaling discharge-first rounding and not buying travel nurses. Do not pause the huddle or defer case managers.
